The first person Jesus ever promised paradise was a criminal, dying on the cross next to him.
And all it took was nine words.
Luke, chapter twenty three.
Golgotha. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle.
On either side, two men Luke calls malefactors.
Mark and Matthew use a sharper Greek word. Laystye. Bandits.
The same word John uses for Barabbas.
The rulers mock him. The soldiers mock him.
Then one of the dying men joins in.
If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.
And here is the strange part.
Mark and Matthew say both of the thieves reviled him.
So how does one of them end up in paradise?
Jerome and John Chrisostom gave the old answer.
At first, both men mocked.
Then, hanging there for hours, one of them changed.
He turns on the other man.
Dust not thou fear God? We receive the due reward of our deeds.
But this man hath done nothing amiss.
Then he turns to Jesus.
Lord, remember me when thou kummest into thy kingdom.
A beaten man, nailed to wood, under a sign mocking him as king.
And he calls him Lord. And talks about his kingdom.
Jesus answers.
Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
Paradise. An old Persian word for a walled royal garden.
The Greek Bible used it for the garden of Eden.
No baptism. No time left. Just a request.
But one comma has divided readers for centuries.
The oldest Greek manuscripts have no commas.
Move the comma after today, and Jesus is only saying when he spoke, not when the man arrives.
Most translations keep it before. The debate never ended.
Centuries later, the Gospel of Nicodemus gave the two men names.
Dizmus, the good thief. And Ghestus, who never asked.
He came to that hill a bandit.
And the last thing he heard was a promise.
